_readme: Declarative rig backend for bg-backup, applied by the BAUER GROUP
minio-init container (ghcr.io/bauer-group/cs-minio/minio-init).
THE INIT POLICY IS THE PRODUCTION POLICY. An over-broad test policy would
hide exactly the class of permission bug that only appears in production -
most obviously the DeleteObject-only-under-locks/ rule, without which restic
leaves a stale lock on every run.
JSON HAS NO COMMENTS, so the rationale lives in _comment / _readme keys.
Both are IGNORED by the init container: tasks/02_policies.py reads only
'name' and 'statements', and an unknown top-level key matches no task's
CONFIG_KEY. Nothing here reaches MinIO except buckets, policies and users.
Never put a _comment INSIDE a statement - that object is sent to IAM
verbatim and an unknown key makes MinIO reject the whole policy.
Placeholders written as a dollar sign followed by {NAME} are resolved from
the init container's environment, and an UNSET variable is a hard error
(main.py: resolve_env_vars raises), so a typo fails the rig instead of
silently creating a user whose name is the placeholder text.
AND THAT RESOLVER IS NOT COMMENT-AWARE: resolve_config_values recurses over
every string in this file, these _readme lines included. Writing a literal
dollar-brace example in prose aborts the whole rig with
Error loading config: Environment variable 'VAR' is not set
which is why the placeholder syntax is spelled out in words here.
CAVEAT that up.sh exists to cover: tasks/02_policies.py logs a failed
'mc admin policy create' in red but does NOT raise, so process_config()
counts it as applied and the container still exits 0. Never treat this
container's exit code as proof that the policy is in place - up.sh
re-reads the attachment from the server and that check is load-bearing.

policies.name: bgb-scoped
_comment: Least privilege for ONE host's repository prefix, shaped exactly like
the production policy (one repository per host prefix in a shared
bucket).
ONLY s3:ListBucket accepts an s3:prefix condition. GetBucketLocation
and ListBucketMultipartUploads are bucket-level operations that take no
prefix, and MinIO rejects the ENTIRE policy with
unsupported condition keys '[s3:prefix]' used for action '<action>'
if either is grouped under the prefix condition. They therefore keep
their own, unconditioned statement - this split is not cosmetic.
DeleteObject is granted ONLY under <prefix>/locks/. restic writes a lock
object on every run and removes it on exit: deny deletes outright and
every run leaves a stale lock behind, and by the third run the
repository needs an unlock that also cannot succeed. Granting delete
repository-wide would make the append-only premise a fiction.

policies.name: bgb-scoped-prune
_comment: The SEPARATE PRUNE IDENTITY of ADR-0005. Backup runs as bgb-scoped and
cannot delete data; only this identity can, and only inside the same
prefix. Keeping it as its own MinIO user is what makes the maintenance
e2e able to prove the split rather than assert it in a document: the
backup user must FAIL to prune, and this user must succeed.

users._comment: The backup identity. Cannot delete anything but its own locks.

_comment: The prune identity of ADR-0005. Never configured for backup jobs.
There is deliberately NO third identity for the copy target. restic
takes its S3 credentials from one set of AWS_* variables, and
lib/retention.sh cmd_copy only overrides RESTIC_REPOSITORY and
RESTIC_FROM_REPOSITORY - so both sides of an S3-to-S3 copy authenticate
as the PRIMARY. Minting a scoped secondary user here would have created
a credential nothing could use, and widening the primary to reach the
copy would defeat the purpose of having one. The maintenance suite
therefore copies to the rest-server, whose auth travels in the URL.
